claims.arxiv2608_25585: A vision-language-action manipulation policy can adapt at test time to task families left out of its adaptation training, using expert demonstrations supplied as context rather than any weight update. What is at stake is both how well it executes the novel task and how its inference cost scales, in simulation and on real hardware. Accepted only if mean whole-task success exceeds that of the strongest earlier in-context imitation policy, under equal training and equal expert-context budgets, in both settings, while the growth in inference latency per additional expert segment is lower than that policy's growth.
claims.arxiv2608_25585_c1: Existing in-context imitation policies for these models adapt poorly for two specific reasons: their retrieval picks context that looks similar rather than context that behaves similarly, and their action predictions barely depend on the retrieved context at all. Dependence is measured as the size of the change in generated actions when relevant context is swapped for random context, relative to the size of the action generated with relevant context, read together with held-out whole-task success. Accepted only if, holding the policy fixed, behaviour-matched retrieval both returns a higher share of cross-demonstration neighbours from the corresponding phase of the motion and yields higher held-out success than appearance-based retrieval, and if existing policies show both lower context dependence and lower held-out success than a comparable policy built to attend to its context.

0.text: Set up the held-out-task evaluation. Setup: one shared 3B-class vision-language-action backbone for every method, dual-view RGB from a third-person and a wrist camera, action horizon 16, four denoising steps, one retrieved expert segment by default. In simulation, four task suites of ten tasks each with 50 demonstrations per task; train on three suites and hold out the fourth entirely, give each held-out task three demonstrations, and measure success over 50 trials. On real hardware, 30 teleoperated demonstrations for each of four tasks; train on three plus simulation data as auxiliary, hold out the fourth, give four demonstrations, and run 12 trials per task. Every method draws from the same demonstration buffer.

1.text: Build the retrieval and execution components under comparison. Setup: cut demonstrations into length-16 action segments at stride 4; align pairs of demonstrations of the same task by time-warping their action sequences; train a two-layer retrieval transformer with a contrastive objective on that alignment. Fine-tune the action head on a mix of relevant retrieved segments and randomly sampled irrelevant ones with a margin term, and initialise the noisy action chunk from the mean action of the retrieved segments. Baselines are the plain policy and three published in-context approaches.

2.text: Novel-task adaptation in simulation. Setup: train on three suites, evaluate on the excluded one with three demonstrations per held-out task and 50 trials. Result: with an off-the-shelf visual retriever the three baselines average 0.045, 0.089 and 0.047 success. Swapping in the action-aware retriever lifts them to 0.124, 0.130 and 0.209, so the retriever alone is worth a lot to the baselines too. The full method averages 0.385, against 0.209 for the strongest baseline under the same retriever, a margin of 0.176; the plain policy averages 0.017.

3.text: The same test on a real arm. Setup: leave-one-task-out across four tasks, all methods given the action-aware retriever, four demonstrations for the held-out task, 12 trials each. Result: whole-task success averages 0.083 for the plain policy, 0.125 and 0.354 for two baselines, and 0.563 for the full method, a margin of 0.208 over the strongest baseline. First-subgoal rates are much closer (0.667 against 0.750 on average), so most of the gap is in finishing rather than starting the task.

4.text: Do the generated actions actually depend on the retrieved context? Setup: on 1,000 samples, compute the norm of the difference between actions generated with retrieved context and with random context, divided by the norm of the action generated with retrieved context, and pair it with held-out success. Result: 0.025 for one baseline and 0.079 for another, against 0.364 for the full method; success tracks it at 0.104, 0.206 and 0.532. Removing the method's context-adherence term drops dependence to 0.035 and success to 0.098, close to baseline levels, so the two move together.

5.text: Does the learned retriever match behaviour rather than appearance? Setup: for each segment of one expert trajectory, retrieve its nearest segment from a second trajectory of the same task, comparing the action-aware retriever with two off-the-shelf visual encoders. Result: the visual encoders return segments from behaviourally different phases of the trajectory while the action-aware one matches corresponding phases. Quantitatively, swapping the retriever on one suite raises success from 10.2% to 53.2% with the policy otherwise unchanged.

7.text: How does inference cost grow with more expert context? Setup: on one A100, generate a single action chunk with four denoising steps and average latency over 1,000 runs at each context size. Result: the baselines' latency climbs steeply as segments are concatenated into the prompt, while this method stays nearly flat because segments are encoded separately and cached. The comparison is reported as a trend only; no latency-growth slopes are given in the text, so the claim's 'lower growth' bar rests on the shape of the curve rather than a number.

notes: Whole paper visible at 18 pages.
